name: Definition of a Parabola
chapter: Grade 12, Selective Compulsory Volume 1, Chapter 3: Equations of Conic Sections, Section 3.3
description: A parabola is the locus of points in a plane that are equally distant from a fixed point and a fixed line. The point is the focus, and the line is the directrix.
mastery_criteria: State the equal-distance condition in the definition of a parabola
Distinguish the focus from the directrix

diagnostic_question.question: Which two distances are compared in the definition of a parabola?
diagnostic_question.answer: the distance to the focus and the distance to the directrix

name: Standard Equation of a Parabola
chapter: Grade 12, Selective Compulsory Volume 1, Chapter 3: Equations of Conic Sections, Section 3.3
description: A parabola with vertex at the origin and focus on the positive x-axis has equation y²=2px (p>0) and focus (p/2,0).
mastery_criteria: Find the focus coordinates from 2p
Determine the direction in which a parabola opens

diagnostic_question.question: For the parabola y²=8x, what is the x-coordinate of its focus?

standards.note: The textbook separates this requirement into practice items. Needs verification.

name: Basic Geometric Properties of a Parabola
chapter: Grade 12, Selective Compulsory Volume 1, Chapter 3: Equations of Conic Sections, Section 3.3
description: For y²=2px (p>0), the range is x≥0, the axis of symmetry is the x-axis, and the directrix is x=−p/2.
mastery_criteria: Write the directrix equation
State the axis of symmetry and range

diagnostic_question.question: For the parabola y²=8x, what is x in the directrix equation?

standards.note: The textbook separates this requirement into practice items. Needs verification.

name: Simple Applications of Parabolas
chapter: Grade 12, Selective Compulsory Volume 1, Chapter 3: Equations of Conic Sections, Section 3.3
description: Parabolas are often used for the cross-sections of searchlights and satellite dishes; rays parallel to the axis converge at the focus.
mastery_criteria: Find the focus from a cross-section equation
Use the definition to compare distances to the focus and directrix

diagnostic_question.question: A satellite-dish cross-section is y²=16x, with units in meters. What is the distance from the focus to the vertex?

standards.note: The textbook separates this requirement into practice items. Needs verification.

name: Number of Intersections of a Line and an Ellipse
chapter: Grade 12, Selective Compulsory Volume 1, Chapter 3: Equations of Conic Sections, Section 3.3
description: Substitute the line into the ellipse equation. The number of real roots of the resulting quadratic equals the number of intersections of the line and ellipse.
mastery_criteria: Substitute a line into an ellipse equation
Determine the number of intersections from the number of real roots

diagnostic_question.question: How many intersections are there between the ellipse x²/4+y²/3=1 and the line y=x?

standards.note: The curriculum requires studying ellipses with equations and solving simple applications. Counting intersections of a line and ellipse is a basic form of this requirement; harder chord-length problems are not listed separately. Needs verification.

name: Concept of a Sequence
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.1
description: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers, and each term has a definite index.
mastery_criteria: Recognize that order matters in a sequence
Identify a term by its index

diagnostic_question.question: Which statement best distinguishes a sequence from a set?
diagnostic_question.answer: Order matters in a sequence, but not in a set

name: Representing Sequences
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.1
description: A sequence can be represented by listing its terms, using a general-term formula, or drawing a graph. Its graph consists of isolated points.
mastery_criteria: Read a specified term from a list
Recognize that a sequence graph is not a continuous curve

diagnostic_question.question: The general term is a_n=2n+1. What is the fourth term?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: General-Term Formula
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.1
description: A general-term formula expresses the nth term in terms of its index n. Once the formula is known, any specified term can be found.
mastery_criteria: Substitute an index into a general-term formula
Find a simple general term from the first few terms

diagnostic_question.question: a_n=3n−1. What is a_4?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Simple Recurrence Relations
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.1
description: A recurrence expresses later terms using earlier terms. Given the first term and the recurrence, the sequence can be calculated term by term.
mastery_criteria: Find the next term from the first term and a recurrence
Distinguish a general-term formula from a recurrence

diagnostic_question.question: a_1=3, a_{n+1}=a_n+4. What is a_2?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Definition of an Arithmetic Sequence
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.2
description: A sequence is arithmetic if, from the second term onward, the difference between each term and the previous term is the same constant. This constant is the common difference.
mastery_criteria: Determine whether a sequence is arithmetic
Find the common difference

diagnostic_question.question: What is the common difference of 3, 7, 11, 15?

name: General Term of an Arithmetic Sequence
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.2
description: For an arithmetic sequence with first term a1 and common difference d, the general term is a_n=a1+(n−1)d.
mastery_criteria: Find a specified term from the first term and common difference
Find the common difference from two terms

diagnostic_question.question: An arithmetic sequence has a_1=3 and d=4. What is a_6?

name: Arithmetic Mean
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.2
description: If a, b, c form an arithmetic sequence, then 2b=a+c, and b is the arithmetic mean of a and c.
mastery_criteria: Find the arithmetic mean from the two endpoints
Determine whether three numbers form an arithmetic sequence

diagnostic_question.question: What is the arithmetic mean of 5 and 11?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Sum of the First n Terms of an Arithmetic Sequence
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.2
description: The sum of the first n terms is S_n=n(a1+a_n)/2, or equivalently S_n=na1+n(n−1)d/2.
mastery_criteria: Find the sum of the first n terms from the first and last terms
Find the sum of the first n terms from the first term and common difference

diagnostic_question.question: An arithmetic sequence has a_1=3 and a_6=23. What is the sum of the first 6 terms?

name: Arithmetic Sequences and Linear Functions
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.2
description: The general term a_n=dn+(a1−d) of an arithmetic sequence is a linear function of n, and the common difference is the coefficient of n.
mastery_criteria: Write a general term as a linear function
Read the common difference from the coefficient of n

diagnostic_question.question: The general term is a_n=4n−1. What is the common difference?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Applications of Arithmetic Sequences
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.2
description: Savings that increase by a fixed amount each period and the number of seats in successive rows can often be modeled by arithmetic sequences.
mastery_criteria: Recognize a fixed increase per period as the common difference
Find a specified term or the sum of the first several terms

diagnostic_question.question: A theater has 20 seats in the first row, with 2 more seats in each following row. How many seats are in the sixth row?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Definition of a Geometric Sequence
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.3
description: A sequence is geometric if, from the second term onward, the ratio of each term to the previous term is the same nonzero constant. This constant is the common ratio.
mastery_criteria: Determine whether a sequence is geometric
Find the common ratio

diagnostic_question.question: What is the common ratio of 2, 6, 18, 54?

name: General Term of a Geometric Sequence
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.3
description: For a geometric sequence with first term a1 and common ratio q, the general term is a_n=a1·q^(n−1).
mastery_criteria: Find a specified term from the first term and common ratio
Find the common ratio from two terms

diagnostic_question.question: A geometric sequence has a_1=2 and q=3. What is a_4?

name: Geometric Mean
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.3
description: If a, G, b form a geometric sequence and have the same sign, then G²=ab. G is the geometric mean of a and b.
mastery_criteria: Find the geometric mean of two positive numbers
Distinguish a geometric mean from an arithmetic mean

diagnostic_question.question: What is the positive geometric mean of 2 and 8?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Sum of the First n Terms of a Geometric Sequence
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.3
description: When q≠1, S_n=a1(q^n−1)/(q−1). When q=1, S_n=na1.
mastery_criteria: Use the sum formula when the common ratio is not 1
Recognize that the case q=1 must be handled separately

diagnostic_question.question: A geometric sequence has a_1=2 and q=3. What is the sum of the first 4 terms?

name: Geometric Sequences and Exponential Functions
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.3
description: The general term a_n=a1·q^(n−1) of a geometric sequence is exponential in form, with the common ratio as its base.
mastery_criteria: Identify the common ratio as the exponential base
Compare the domains of a geometric sequence and an exponential function

diagnostic_question.question: The general term is a_n=3×2^(n−1). What is the common ratio?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Applications of Geometric Sequences
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.3
description: Quantities that grow or shrink by the same ratio can be modeled by geometric sequences.
mastery_criteria: Recognize a fixed growth rate as a common ratio
Find a quantity after several periods

diagnostic_question.question: A bacteria population doubles each hour. If it starts at 3, how many bacteria are there after 3 hours?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Principle of Mathematical Induction
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.4
description: Mathematical induction first verifies the base case, then proves that if the statement holds for n=k, it also holds for n=k+1. This establishes it for all positive integers.
mastery_criteria: State the two steps of induction
Recognize that checking only a few specific values is not a proof

diagnostic_question.question: What is usually the first step of mathematical induction?

standards.note: The Teacher's Home outline marks Section 4.4, Mathematical Induction, with an asterisk, which usually indicates optional material. The curriculum standard requires familiarity with the principle; whether it is compulsory is unverified.

name: Proving Simple Statements by Induction
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 4: Sequences, Section 4.4
description: To prove an identity involving positive integers, state the base case and show the steps from k to k+1.
mastery_criteria: Verify the base case
Use the induction hypothesis in the inductive step

diagnostic_question.question: The sum of the first n positive integers is n(n+1)/2. What is the sum when n=5?

name: Average Rate of Change
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.1
description: The average rate of change of a function over an interval is the change in its function values divided by the change in its input values.
mastery_criteria: Calculate the average rate of change on a given interval
Identify the average rate of change as the slope of a secant line

diagnostic_question.question: For f(x)=x², what is the average rate of change from x=1 to x=3?

name: Instantaneous Rate of Change and the Limit Idea
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.1
description: As the change in the input approaches 0, the limit of the average rate of change is the instantaneous rate of change. Specific rational values are used here to illustrate the process.
mastery_criteria: Recognize the instantaneous rate of change as the limit of average rates of change
Use smaller input changes to observe the average rate of change

diagnostic_question.question: For f(x)=x², what is the average rate of change from x=2 to x=2.5?

standards.note: The limit idea appears in the development of the derivative concept; limit calculations are not treated separately. Pending verification.

name: Definition of a Derivative
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.1
description: The derivative of a function at a point is its instantaneous rate of change there. The derivative is itself a function of the input, denoted f'(x).
mastery_criteria: Recognize the derivative as the instantaneous rate of change
Calculate the derivative value of a basic power function at a point

diagnostic_question.question: For f(x)=x², f'(x)=2x. What is f'(3)?

name: Derivative Function
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.1
description: Collecting the derivative values at all points gives the derivative function. The original function and its derivative may have different domains.
mastery_criteria: Find a derivative at a point from the derivative function
Distinguish f(x) from f'(x)

diagnostic_question.question: f'(x)=3x²−3. What is f'(2)?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Geometric Meaning of the Derivative
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.1
description: The derivative of a function at a point is the slope of the tangent to the curve there.
mastery_criteria: Interpret a derivative value as a tangent slope
Recognize that a positive derivative gives an upward-sloping tangent

diagnostic_question.question: The derivative of y=x² at x=1 is 2. What is the tangent slope?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Tangent-Line Equation
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.1
description: The tangent to a curve at (x0, y0) has slope f'(x0); write its equation in point-slope form.
mastery_criteria: Find the slope at a point of tangency
Write the tangent equation in point-slope form and find its intercept

diagnostic_question.question: The tangent to y=x² at (1, 1) has slope 2. What is its y-intercept?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Derivatives of Basic Elementary Functions
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.2
description: The derivative of a constant function is 0, and (x^n)'=nx^(n−1). Use this rule to differentiate positive integer powers directly.
mastery_criteria: Differentiate power functions
Recognize that the derivative of a constant function is 0

diagnostic_question.question: For f(x)=x³, what is the derivative function's value at x=2?

name: Derivative Rules for Sums, Differences, and Constant Multiples
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.2
description: The derivative of a sum or difference is the sum or difference of the derivatives. A constant factor can be taken outside the derivative.
mastery_criteria: Differentiate a polynomial term by term
Differentiate a constant multiple of a function

diagnostic_question.question: f(x)=x²+3x. What is f'(1)?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Derivatives of Simple Composite Functions
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.2
description: For a function of the form f(ax+b), the derivative is the outer derivative multiplied by the inner coefficient a.
mastery_criteria: Differentiate f(ax+b)
Multiply the outer derivative by the coefficient a

diagnostic_question.question: y=(2x+1)². What is the derivative at x=1?

standards.note: The curriculum standard requires only composites of the form f(ax+b). Pending verification.

name: Derivatives and Monotonicity
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.3
description: A function is increasing on an interval where f'(x)>0 and decreasing where f'(x)<0.
mastery_criteria: Determine whether a function increases or decreases from the sign of its derivative
Recognize that isolated points where the derivative is 0 do not change monotonicity on the whole interval

diagnostic_question.question: f(x)=x² and f'(x)=2x. What is f'(−1)?

name: Finding Intervals of Monotonicity with Derivatives
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.3
description: Differentiate first, then solve f'(x)>0 and f'(x)<0 to find the intervals of monotonicity for polynomial functions of degree at most 3.
mastery_criteria: Find the derivative of a polynomial
Write the solution set of f'(x)>0 as an interval of increase

diagnostic_question.question: f(x)=x²−4x. What is x when f'(x)=0?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Conditions for Local Extrema
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.3
description: A zero derivative is a necessary condition for a differentiable function to have an extremum. A change in the derivative's sign across the point is sufficient.
mastery_criteria: Find points where the derivative is 0
Distinguish local maxima from local minima using the signs on either side

diagnostic_question.question: For f(x)=x²−4x+1, what is the x-coordinate of a possible extremum?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Absolute Extrema on a Closed Interval
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.3
description: A continuous function on a closed interval attains its maximum and minimum at a local extremum or an endpoint. Compare the function values at these points.
mastery_criteria: List the local extrema and endpoints
Compare function values to find the maximum or minimum

diagnostic_question.question: What is the maximum of f(x)=x²−2x on [0, 3]?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate sections. Pending verification.

name: Optimization with Derivatives
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.3
description: Express area, profit, or another quantity as a function, then use derivatives to find its maximum or minimum on the domain.
mastery_criteria: Express practical constraints as a function and its domain
Use derivatives to find an optimal value

diagnostic_question.question: A rectangle has perimeter 20. Its area is greatest when its sides are equal. What is the maximum area?

name: Polynomial Functions of Degree at Most 3
chapter: Grade 13, Selective Compulsory Volume 2, Chapter 5: Derivatives and Their Applications for One-Variable Functions, Section 5.3
description: The curriculum standard requires using derivatives to study polynomials of degree at most 3. The derivative of a cubic polynomial is quadratic.
mastery_criteria: Differentiate a cubic polynomial
Find points where the derivative is 0

diagnostic_question.question: f(x)=x³−3x+1. What is f'(0)?

standards.note: The curriculum standard limits the study of monotonicity and extrema to polynomials of degree at most 3. Pending verification.

name: Addition Principle for Counting
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.1
description: If an activity can be completed using one of several mutually exclusive categories of methods, the total number of methods is the sum of the counts in each category.
mastery_criteria: Determine when to count by mutually exclusive cases and add
Count the total number of methods across mutually exclusive categories

diagnostic_question.question: There are 3 bus services and 2 train services from Town A to Town B. A traveler can use only one mode. How many ways are there to travel?

name: Multiplication Principle for Counting
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.1
description: If an activity requires several successive steps, multiply the number of choices at each step to get the total number of methods.
mastery_criteria: Determine when to count by successive steps and multiply
Calculate the product of the number of choices at each step

diagnostic_question.question: There are 3 shirts and 4 pairs of pants. Choosing one of each gives how many outfits?

name: Combined Case and Step Counting
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.1
description: When a problem involves both cases and successive steps, identify which counts should be added and which should be multiplied, then combine them.
mastery_criteria: Use both addition and multiplication in one counting problem
Write a counting expression step by step

diagnostic_question.question: Choose 1 representative from 3 boys and 2 girls, then give that person 1 of 4 notebooks. How many ways can this be done?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate parts. To verify.

name: Concept of a Permutation
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.2
description: A permutation is an ordered arrangement of k elements selected from n distinct elements. Different orders count as different permutations.
mastery_criteria: Explain that permutations depend on order
Calculate small permutation counts

diagnostic_question.question: Which situation is a permutation?
diagnostic_question.answer: Choose 2 of 4 students and arrange them in order

name: Permutation Formula
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.2
description: The number of permutations is A(n,k)=n!/(n−k)!, the product of k consecutive decreasing integers starting at n.
mastery_criteria: Calculate permutation counts
Explain the permutation formula

diagnostic_question.question: What is A(6,2)?

name: Simple Applications of Permutations
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.2
description: Count queues, assignments to distinct roles, and numbers with no repeated digits as ordered selections.
mastery_criteria: Determine whether a practical problem involves permutations
Use a permutation count to express the result

diagnostic_question.question: Five students line up for a photo, and everyone must stand in line. How many lineups are possible?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate parts. To verify.

name: Concept of a Combination
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.2
description: A combination is a selection of k elements from n distinct elements where only the selected elements matter, not their order.
mastery_criteria: Distinguish combinations from permutations
Calculate small combination counts

diagnostic_question.question: Which situation is a combination?
diagnostic_question.answer: Choose 2 of 4 students to attend a meeting, without assigning an order

name: Combination Formula
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.2
description: The number of combinations is C(n,k)=n!/(k!(n−k)!), or the permutation count divided by k factorial.
mastery_criteria: Calculate combination counts
Know that C(n,0)=1

diagnostic_question.question: What is C(6,2)?

name: Properties of Combination Numbers
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.2
description: Combination numbers satisfy C(n,k)=C(n,n−k) and the adjacent-term identity C(n,k)+C(n,k−1)=C(n+1,k).
mastery_criteria: Use symmetry to calculate combination numbers
Check combination numbers using the addition identity

diagnostic_question.question: Given C(8,3)=C(8,5), what is C(8,5)?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate parts. To verify.

name: Simple Applications of Combinations
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.2
description: Use combinations when selecting people or objects without regard to order. If selections are made separately by category, multiply the combination counts.
mastery_criteria: Determine when a practical problem calls for combinations rather than permutations
Calculate combination counts for selections by category

diagnostic_question.question: How many ways can 3 of 6 students be selected for an activity when order does not matter?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate parts. To verify.

name: Binomial Theorem
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.3
description: The expansion of (a+b)^n is the sum of terms C(n,k) a^(n−k) b^k, with k ranging from 0 to n.
mastery_criteria: State the number of terms in an expansion
Find the binomial coefficient of a specified term

diagnostic_question.question: What is the coefficient of x² in the expansion of (1+x)^3?

name: Specified Terms in a Binomial Expansion
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.3
description: When terms are arranged in descending powers of a, term k+1 is C(n,k) a^(n−k) b^k. The exponents can be used to find k.
mastery_criteria: Find k from an exponent
Calculate the coefficient of a specified term, including its factor

diagnostic_question.question: In (a+b)^5 arranged in descending powers of a, what is the binomial coefficient of the third term?

name: Sum of Binomial Coefficients
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 6: Counting Principles, Section 6.3
description: Setting a=b=1 shows that the sum of the binomial coefficients is 2^n.
mastery_criteria: Calculate the sum of a row of binomial coefficients
Explain why the sum is 2 to the power n

diagnostic_question.question: What is the sum of all the binomial coefficients in (a+b)^4?

standards.note: The textbook practices this requirement in separate parts. To verify.

name: Properties of Pascal's Triangle
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Integrated Practice: Properties and Applications of Pascal's Triangle
description: Row n of Pascal's triangle, counting from row 0, contains the binomial coefficients of (a+b)^n. The row is symmetric, and the sum of adjacent entries gives an entry in the next row.
mastery_criteria: Read an entry of Pascal's triangle using the stated indexing
Explain the sum of adjacent entries using combination numbers

diagnostic_question.question: Arrange the binomial coefficients of (a+b)^n in a row, with n starting at 0. What is the third entry from the left in row n=5 (corresponding to k=2)?

name: Conditional Probability
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.1
description: The probability of event A given that event B has occurred is P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B).
mastery_criteria: Calculate conditional probability in a restricted sample space
State the definition of conditional probability

diagnostic_question.question: A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue balls. One red ball has been drawn without replacement. What is the probability that the next ball is red?

name: Multiplication Rule for Probability
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.1
description: P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B|A). Probabilities can be multiplied in the order that events occur.
mastery_criteria: Use the multiplication rule to calculate the probability of two events occurring together
Write conditional probabilities in event order

diagnostic_question.question: P(A)=1/2 and P(B|A)=1/3. What is the probability that both A and B occur?

name: Law of Total Probability
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.1
description: If several mutually exclusive causes cover all possibilities, an event's probability is the sum of each cause's probability multiplied by the corresponding conditional probability.
mastery_criteria: Partition a sample space into mutually exclusive cases
Calculate total probability

diagnostic_question.question: Box A contains 2 red and 1 white ball; Box B contains 1 red and 2 white balls. A box is chosen at random, then one ball is drawn. What is the probability of drawing a red ball?

name: Bayes' Theorem
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.1
description: Given that an outcome has occurred, use its total probability as the denominator to find the probability that it came from a particular cause.
mastery_criteria: Calculate the probability of a cause given an observed outcome
Identify the denominator as the total probability of that outcome

diagnostic_question.question: Machine A makes 3/5 of all products and has a defect rate of 1/10; machine B makes 2/5 and has a defect rate of 1/5. Given that a selected item is defective, what is the probability it came from A?

name: Conditional Probability and Independence
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.1
description: If P(B|A)=P(B), then A does not change the probability of B, and A and B are independent. Independence is not the same as mutual exclusivity.
mastery_criteria: Use conditional probability to test independence
Distinguish independence from mutual exclusivity

diagnostic_question.question: Events A and B are independent, and P(B)=1/3. What is P(B|A)?

name: Discrete Random Variables
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.2
description: A random variable assigns a real number to each outcome of an experiment. It is discrete if it takes a finite or countable set of values.
mastery_criteria: Identify the possible values of a random variable in an experiment
Explain that discreteness depends on the set of possible values

diagnostic_question.question: A fair die is rolled, and X is the number shown. How many distinct values can X take?

name: Probability Distribution
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.2
description: A probability distribution lists each value of a random variable and its corresponding probability. Probabilities are nonnegative and sum to 1.
mastery_criteria: Find a missing probability using the fact that probabilities sum to 1
Check whether a probability distribution is valid

diagnostic_question.question: X takes values 1, 2, and 3. P(X=1)=1/2 and P(X=2)=1/3. What is P(X=3)?

name: Two-Point Distribution
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.2
description: A random variable taking only 0 and 1 has P(X=1)=p and P(X=0)=1−p. It describes success or failure in one trial.
mastery_criteria: Find the failure probability from the success probability
State that the mean of a two-point distribution is p

diagnostic_question.question: X has a two-point distribution with P(X=1)=1/4. What is P(X=0)?

standards.note: A two-point distribution is one example of a probability distribution. To verify.

name: Mean of a Discrete Random Variable
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.3
description: The mean, or expected value, is the sum of each value multiplied by its probability. It is a probability-weighted average.
mastery_criteria: Calculate a mean from a probability distribution
Explain that the mean is a weighted average

diagnostic_question.question: X takes values 1, 2, and 3 with probabilities 1/2, 1/3, and 1/6, respectively. What is the mean of X?

name: Variance of a Discrete Random Variable
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.3
description: Variance is the probability-weighted sum of squared deviations from the mean. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
mastery_criteria: Calculate the variance of a simple distribution
Know that a constant random variable has variance 0

diagnostic_question.question: X takes values 0 and 1, each with probability 1/2. What is its variance?

name: Bernoulli Trials
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.4
description: Each trial has two possible outcomes, the probability of success remains p, and trials are independent. Repeating the trial n times gives n Bernoulli trials.
mastery_criteria: Determine whether a set of trials is Bernoulli
Identify the number of trials and the success probability

diagnostic_question.question: Each independent trial has a success probability of 1/5. What is the probability of failure?

name: Binomial Distribution
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.4
description: In n Bernoulli trials, the number of successes X follows a binomial distribution: P(X=k)=C(n,k) p^k (1−p)^(n−k).
mastery_criteria: Calculate a probability for a binomial distribution
Explain that X is the number of successes

diagnostic_question.question: X follows B(4,1/2). What is P(X=2)?

name: Mean and Variance of a Binomial Distribution
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.4
description: If X follows B(n,p), its mean is np and its variance is np(1−p).
mastery_criteria: Calculate the mean of a binomial distribution
Calculate the variance of a binomial distribution

diagnostic_question.question: X follows B(10,1/5). What is its mean?

name: Hypergeometric Distribution
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.4
description: A population of N items contains K defective items. If n items are drawn without replacement, the number of defectives drawn follows a hypergeometric distribution.
mastery_criteria: Calculate a probability for sampling without replacement
Distinguish a hypergeometric distribution from a binomial distribution with replacement

diagnostic_question.question: A batch of 10 products contains 4 defective items. Three are drawn without replacement. What is the probability of drawing exactly 1 defective item?

name: Mean of a Hypergeometric Distribution
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.4
description: When n items are drawn without replacement, the mean number from a specified category is nK/N.

Explain the meanings of N, K, and n in the formula

diagnostic_question.question: A population has 10 items, 4 in a specified category. If 3 are sampled without replacement, what is the mean number from that category?

name: Properties of the Normal Distribution
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.5
description: A normal curve is a single-peaked bell curve symmetric about its mean. The mean sets its axis of symmetry, and the variance determines its spread.
mastery_criteria: State that a normal curve is symmetric about its mean
Explain that a larger variance makes the curve flatter

diagnostic_question.question: A normal distribution has mean 5. What is the x-coordinate of the normal curve's axis of symmetry?

name: Empirical Rule for the Normal Curve
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 7: Random Variables and Their Distributions, Section 7.5
description: A common textbook approximation is that about 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean and about 95% lie within 2 standard deviations.
mastery_criteria: Identify the interval within 1 standard deviation of the mean
Know that these percentages are approximate empirical rules

diagnostic_question.question: A normal distribution has mean 10 and standard deviation 2. How many standard deviations is the half-width of the interval within 1 standard deviation of the mean?

standards.note: The 68% and 95% figures are common textbook approximations, not exact calculations. To verify.

name: Statistical Correlation of Paired Data
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 8: Statistical Analysis of Paired Data, Section 8.1
description: Plot paired data as a scatterplot. Points trending upward along a line indicate positive correlation; points trending downward indicate negative correlation.
mastery_criteria: Determine positive or negative correlation from the scatterplot trend
Know that correlation is not an exact functional relationship

diagnostic_question.question: What does a scatterplot trending roughly from the lower left to the upper right indicate?

name: Sample Correlation Coefficient
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 8: Statistical Analysis of Paired Data, Section 8.1
description: The sample correlation coefficient r uses products of deviations to measure the direction and strength of linear correlation. Its value lies between −1 and 1.
mastery_criteria: Calculate the sum of products of deviations for a small data set
Know that linear correlation is strong when r is near 1 or −1

diagnostic_question.question: For the data (1, 2), (2, 4), and (3, 6), the means of x and y are 2 and 4. What is the sum of the products of deviations?

name: Comparing Correlation Strength
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 8: Statistical Analysis of Paired Data, Section 8.1
description: Compare the strength of linear correlation using |r|. A larger absolute value indicates stronger linear correlation; the sign indicates only its direction.
mastery_criteria: Compare two correlation coefficients using absolute value
Distinguish correlation direction from strength

diagnostic_question.question: Two sample correlation coefficients are −3/5 and 1/5. What is the absolute value of the one indicating stronger linear correlation?

name: Simple Linear Regression Model
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 8: Statistical Analysis of Paired Data, Section 8.2
description: Simple linear regression expresses a response variable as a linear function of an explanatory variable plus random error.
mastery_criteria: Identify the explanatory and response variables in a model
Find the value on the line when the error is zero

diagnostic_question.question: What is the basic form of a simple linear regression model?
diagnostic_question.answer: The response variable equals a linear function plus random error

name: Least-Squares Principle
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 8: Statistical Analysis of Paired Data, Section 8.2
description: The least-squares method selects the line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals. A residual is the observed value minus the predicted value.
mastery_criteria: Calculate a residual
State that least squares minimizes the sum of squared residuals

diagnostic_question.question: A point has observed value 5 and predicted value 3. What is its residual?

name: Least-Squares Estimates of Regression Coefficients
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 8: Statistical Analysis of Paired Data, Section 8.2
description: For points (x_i,y_i), the slope is b=(n∑xy−∑x∑y)/(n∑x²−(∑x)²), and the intercept is a=ȳ−b x̄.
mastery_criteria: Calculate a slope from a small data set
Then calculate the intercept

diagnostic_question.question: For the points (1, 1), (2, 3), and (3, 5), what is the least-squares slope b?

name: Prediction with a Regression Line
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 8: Statistical Analysis of Paired Data, Section 8.2
description: Substitute a new x into the regression line to obtain a predicted y value. A prediction is an estimate, not a certain observation.
mastery_criteria: Substitute x into a line to find a predicted value
Know that predictions and observations may differ

diagnostic_question.question: A regression line is y=2x−1. What is the predicted y value when x=4?

name: 2×2 Contingency Table
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 8: Statistical Analysis of Paired Data, Section 8.3
description: When each of two categorical variables has two categories, arrange the counts in a 2×2 contingency table and calculate row totals, column totals, and the grand total.
mastery_criteria: Calculate the total in a contingency table
Calculate a row total

diagnostic_question.question: A contingency table has cell counts 10, 6, 4, and 10. What is the total number of observations?

standards.note: The 8.3 section name follows Haoduo E-Textbooks and the Linfen table of contents: 'Contingency Tables and Tests of Independence.' Teacher's Home uses 'Categorical Variables and Contingency Tables.' To verify.

name: Idea Behind the Test of Independence
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 8: Statistical Analysis of Paired Data, Section 8.3
description: A test of independence begins by assuming that two categorical variables are independent, then checks whether the observed contingency table deviates too far from that assumption.
mastery_criteria: Explain that independence is assumed first and deviation is then assessed
Know that ad−bc=0 indicates balance among the four cells

diagnostic_question.question: What assumption is made at the start of a test of independence?
diagnostic_question.answer: The two categorical variables are assumed to be independent

name: Test-of-Independence Statistic
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Compulsory Volume 3, Chapter 8: Statistical Analysis of Paired Data, Section 8.3
description: For a 2×2 table, use χ²=n(ad−bc)²/((a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)). A larger value provides more evidence of an association.
mastery_criteria: Substitute the four cell counts into the formula
Know that a statistic of 0 means the cross-products balance

diagnostic_question.question: A contingency table has a=20, b=5, c=5, and d=20. Using χ²=n(ad−bc)²/((a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)), what is the statistic?

standards.note: This is a common statistic for testing independence in a 2×2 table. Critical-value tables have not been checked against each edition. To verify.

chapter: Grade 14, Selective Required Volume II, Chapter Four: Electromagnetic Oscillations and Waves, Section 4.2
description: Maxwell's electromagnetic field theory: a changing magnetic field produces an electric field, and a changing electric field produces a magnetic field. A uniformly changing field produces a constant field; a periodically changing field produces a periodic field of the same frequency. Changing electromagnetic fields propagate outward as electromagnetic waves. These are transverse waves and travel at speed c in a vacuum, independent of frequency.
mastery_criteria: State Maxwell's two basic propositions and identify the type of field produced
Know that electromagnetic waves are transverse, with E, B, and the direction of propagation mutually perpendicular
Use c = λf to calculate wavelength and frequency

diagnostic_question.question: What is a basic proposition of Maxwell's electromagnetic field theory?
diagnostic_question.answer: A changing magnetic field produces an electric field, and a changing electric field produces a magnetic field

subject: physics

name: Radio Transmission and Reception
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Required Volume II, Chapter Four: Electromagnetic Oscillations and Waves, Section 4.3
description: Radio transmission requires a high-frequency, open LC oscillator. Modulation places signals such as audio on a high-frequency carrier: amplitude modulation changes the amplitude, while frequency modulation changes the frequency. At the receiver, tuning selects a station, and demodulation (detection) extracts the signal.
mastery_criteria: Describe the conditions needed for effective electromagnetic-wave transmission
Distinguish modulation, tuning, and demodulation

name: Electromagnetic Spectrum
chapter: Grade 14, Selective Required Volume II, Chapter Four: Electromagnetic Oscillations and Waves, Section 4.4
description: In order of decreasing wavelength, the electromagnetic spectrum is radio waves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays. They all travel at the same speed in a vacuum; higher frequency means shorter wavelength. Each band has distinct properties and applications.
mastery_criteria: List the electromagnetic spectrum in order of wavelength

diagnostic_question.question: Which sequence correctly orders electromagnetic waves from longest to shortest wavelength?
